L211: # AxonCUDA
L212: 
L213: A hypergraph partitioning tool designed to leverage the massive parallelism of a GPU. Entirely developed in CUDA, every algorithm is parallel in nodes and hyperedge pins, with at most one sequential iteration over incidence sets when visiting neighborhoods.
L214: 
L215: Present algorithms originally targeted a specific set of partitioning constraints:
L216: 
L217:   * maximum nodes per partition
L218:   * maximum distinct inbound hyperedges per partition
L219: However, it has also been generalized to support $k$-way balanced partitioning.
L220: The primary optimization objective is the connectivity (or $\lambda - 1$ metric).
L221: 
L222: A hypergraph placement tool is also part of this project. It expands on the algorithms used for partitioning, assigning nodes of a hypergraph to those of a supporting graph. More details in 【97†the dedicated README】.
L223: ## Requirements
L224: 
L225: Tested with:
L226: 
L227:   * Nvidia drivers: 550.78
L228:   * CUDA version: 12.4
L229:   * GCC 13.4.0
L230:   * GPUs:
L231:     * GH200
L232:     * A100-SXM4-40GB
L233:     * RTX 2080ti
L234:     * A6000
L235: ## Setup
L236: Ensure you have CUDA version >=12.4 and drivers version >=550.54 available. You can set them both up as follows (【98†source†developer.nvidia.com】):
L237: 
L238:     # download CUDA
L239:     wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/12.4.0/local_installers/cuda_12.4.0_550.54.14_linux.run
L240:     # set it up (replace <version> with actual version number)
L241:     sh cuda_<version>_linux.run --silent --toolkit --override --installpath=$HOME/cuda
L242:     # put a link to cuda in this project's path
L243:     ln -s $HOME/cuda/include cuda-include
L244: If you intend to use AxonCUDA for $k$-way partitioning, Mt-KaHyPar is required to produce the initial partitioning. Hence, please set up Mt-KaHyPar following the instructions 【99†here】 regarding the Debian package release. In brief:
L245: 
L246:     # download the package
L247:     wget https://github.com/kahypar/mt-kahypar/releases/download/v1.5.3/mtkahypar_1.5.3_amd64.deb
L248:     # extract it
L249:     dpkg -x mtkahypar_1.5.3_amd64.deb mtkahypar
L250:     # add mtkahypar to path
L251:     export PATH="$HOME/mtkahypar/usr/bin:$PATH"
L252: Then, make sure `mtkahypar` is a valid executable in your environment.
L253: 
L254: Build this project:
L255: 
L256:     # optional: override target compute capability (ex. with 'sm_80')
L257:     sed -i 's/native/sm_80/' makefile
L258:     # straight build
L259:     make clean && make
L260: ## Usage
L261: 
L262: Refer to the help menu `./hgraph_gpu.exe -h` for detailed usage instructions.
L263: 
L264: AxonCUDA supports two partitioning modes. Inbound constrained minimal partitioning, that attempts to construct the fewest partitions under size and inbound set size constraints per partition. K-way balanced partitioning, with a fixed number of partitions and a constraint only on partition size. Both modes optimize for minimum connectivity, but cut-net and SOED also improve as a side-effect (see 【100†metrics】).
L265: Examples of typical invocations are as follows:
L266: 
L267:     # partition a SNN with predefined constraints
L268:     ./hgraph_gpu.exe -r hgraphs/some_snn.snn -c loihi84
L269:     # partition a SNN with custom constraints and algorithm-specific options
L270:     ./hgraph_gpu.exe -r hgraphs/some_snn.snn -m 128 1024 4096 -cnc 4 -rfr 32
L271:     # partition a hypergraph under k-way balanced constraints
L272:     ./hgraph_gpu.exe -r hgraphs/some_hgr.hgr -k 2 0.03
L273: 
L274: Partitioning settings:
L275:   * `-r <hgraph>`: path to the hypergraph to partition;
L276:   * `-c <name>`: choose a named constraints set, among hard-coded ones, for inbound constrained minimal partitioning;
L277:   * `-m <size> <inbound> <p-cnt>`: set partitions size, inbound size, and count constraints for inbound constrained minimal partitioning;
L278:   * `-k <k> <ε>`: set partitions count and balance parameter for k-way balanced partitioning;
L279: 
L280: > Unless `-k` is present, the partitioning mode defaults to inbound constrained minimal partitioning.
L281: Recommended options:
L282: 
L283:   * `-dtc`: speed up loading time by building and deduplicating initial incidence sets directly on the GPU;
L284:   * `-ipm`: speed up refinement by reducing the number of initial partitions through greedy merging;
L285: 
L286: Helpful options:
L287: 
L288:   * `-smh <lvl>`: increasing 'lvl' can prevent going out of memory when there are many coarsening levels or simply many nodes/nets;
L289:   * `-om <mult>`: do increase iff an assert for full hash tables triggers during initial neighbors construction;
L290: ## Procuring Hypergraphs
L291: 
L292: Our set of benchmark hypergraphs derived from Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) is available 【101†here (Zenodo)†zenodo.org】.
L293: 
L294: Other relevant benchmarks are the ISPD98 suite and SAT14 suite, that we suggest downloading from 【102†here (Zenodo)†zenodo.org】.
L295: Their size is however relatively small to represent a challenge on GPU, hence we provide the `scale_hgr.py` slop-script to multiply their number of nodes and pins by a user-defined amount (e.g. 16x).
L296: AxonCUDA supports hypergraphs both in the `.hgr` and in its own `.snn` and `.axh` binary formats.
L297: File format details can be found in comments near the end of 【103†`hgraph.hpp`】.
L298: 
L299: Or you could just go under 【104†`hgraphs`】 and run:
L300: 
L301:     # fetch all hypergraphs (expected space required: 33GB of SNNs + 1GB of ISPD98)
L302:     ./procure_hgraphs.sh
L303: # Some Terminology
L304: ## Algorithmic Complexity Legend
L305: 
L306: A hypergraph (hgraph) is defined as $G = (N, E, \omega)$, where $N = {0, 1, \dots, n - 1}$ is the set of vertices, or nodes, and $n = |N|$. The hyperedge set is $E = {(s, D) \mid s \in N, D \subseteq N}$, where each hyperedge has a source $src(e)$, a set of destinations $dst(e)$ (no self-cycles), and a weight given by $\omega : E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.
L307: Be $P \subseteq \mathcal{P}(N)$ a partitioning of $N$, equivalently defined by a function $\rho : N \rightarrow P$ assigning nodes to partitions.
L308: 
L309: Let $\Omega$ be the maximum number of nodes allowed for a partition, and $\Delta$ its maximum number of distinct inbound hyperedges. Formally, our constraints imply:
L310: 
L311: $$\begin{aligned} \forall b \in P, \: |b| &\leq \Omega \\\ |\textstyle\bigcup_{u \in b} in(u)| &\leq \Delta \end{aligned}$$
L312: For convenience, we discuss algorithmic complexity using the following variables w.r.t. a generic hgraph:
L313: 
L314:   * $n$ : number of hgraph nodes, $|N|$
L315:   * $e$ : number of hgraph hedges, $|E|$
L316:   * $d$ : average cardinality of each hedge, $\sum_{\eta \in E} |\eta| / |E|$
L317:   * $h$ : average connections per node (node degree), $(\sum_{u \in N} |{\eta \in E \mid u \in \eta}|) / |N| = e \cdot d / n$
L318:   * $p$ : number of achieved partitions, $|P|$
L319: ## Hypergraph Partitioning Metrics
L320: 
L321: Let $G = (N, E, \omega)$ be a hypergraph with node set $N$, where $n = |N|$; for metric definitions, each hyperedge $e \in E$ is identified with its incident node set $e \subseteq N$. Each hyperedge has weight $\omega(e)$, where $\omega : E \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. Let $P = {p_1, \dots, p_k} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(N)$ be a partition of $N$. For a hyperedge $e \in E$, define its connectivity as
L322: 
L323: $$\lambda(e) = \left|\{\, i \mid e \cap p_i \neq \emptyset \,\}\right|.$$
L324: Then a partition's quality metrics are:
L325: 
L326: Cut Size (Cut-Net) | Counts the number of hyperedges that span more than one block (i.e. are cut):
L327: 
L328: $$\text{CutSize} = \sum_{e \in E} \omega(e) \cdot \mathbf{1}\{\lambda(e) > 1\}.$$
L329: 
L330: * * *
L331: 
L332: Connectivity (km1) | Sums the excess connectivity of each hyperedge:
L333: 
L334: $$\text{Conn} = \sum_{e \in E} \omega(e) \cdot \bigl(\lambda(e) - 1\bigr).$$
L335: 
L336: * * *
L337: 
L338: Sum of External Degrees (SOED) | Weights excess connectivity by hyperedge size:
L339: $$\text{SOED} = \sum_{e \in E} \omega(e) \cdot |e| \cdot \bigl(\lambda(e) - 1\bigr).$$
L340: ## Speaking of Gains
L341: 
L342: We refer to refinement gains in two ways:
L343: 
L344:   * in-isolation: gain calculated for a move applied by itself
L345:   * in-sequence: gain for a move calculated assuming all higher-gain moves already applied
L346:

L372: # Oopsies
L373: 
L374: Well, this implementation isn't bulletproof, there are a few knobs that require tuning upon targeting very large hypergraphs. All problems manifest as asserts being triggered:
L375:   * `idx < extra_path_size + path_size` in `grouping_kernel`:
L376:     * try increasing `PATH_SIZE`, but keep in mind that it should fit in a thread's registers for performance reasons...
L377:     * check how many repeats the kernel is running, e.g. `NOTE: grouping kernel required [...] repeats=42 ...`, the number of repeats is actively shrinking the available path-length, hence try multiplying `PATH_SIZE` by the same amount...
L378:     * if even with `PATH_SIZE = 1024` the problem persist, the likely suspect is an asymmetric neighbors histogram from `candidates_kernel`, run with `-v 3` for more info. That said, bugs aside, the only reasonable cause is an overflow due to `FIXED_POINT_SCALE`, try lowering it...
L379:   * `GM hash-set full!` in any `apply_X` or `neighbors` kernel means oversized segments for deduplication were not large enough, increase `-om <mul>` from the CLI...
L380:   * `invalid partitioning returned` in k-way mode after the initial Mt-KaHyPar solution means no valid initial partitioning likely existed, try raising `KWAY_INIT_UPPER_THREASHOLD`...
L381:   * in case of an unexpected `invalid partitioning` under known valid constraints:
L382:     * inspect the total hyperedge weight (printed after the hypergraph is loaded), and if it is close to the `uint32 / FIXED_POINT_SCALE` limit, the cause is likely an overflow after applying `FIXED_POINT_SCALE`, try lowering it...
L383:     * otherwise, make sure the hypergraph has less than $2^{32}$ nodes or hyperedges, as the code is currently hardwired to identify those with 32 bits...
L384:   * too much host RAM usage: add the `-dtc` flag if your device has more VRAM than the host has RAM! Also recommended for a good speedup...
L385: > After any modification, remember to recompile (`make`)!
L386: 
L387: All mentioned constants can be found either in 【105†`defines.cuh`】 or in the offending kernel's header file under 【106†`./headers`】.
